reason: Richly documented mystery supported across multiple space agency and science news sources with numerous multi-verified data points.
story: At the center of galaxy cluster Abell 2261 sits A2261-BCG, an elliptical monster galaxy spanning one million light-years across—ten times the size of the Milky Way. Given its colossal mass, astronomers calculated its core should harbor an absolute titan of a supermassive black hole weighing between 3 billion and 100 billion solar masses. But when telescopes looked inside, they found an eerie cosmic ghost town. The galaxy possesses a bloated, diffuse core 10,000 light-years across with no central peak of starlight. Deeper observations by the Hubble Space Telescope and Chandra X-ray Observatory failed to detect any telltale X-rays from an active black hole. The prime suspect? An ancient galactic collision where two supermassive black holes merged, generating lopsided gravitational waves that acted like a cosmic rocket engine, completely ejecting the multi-billion-solar-mass monster out of its host galaxy into intergalactic space.
angle: A monstrous supermassive black hole weighing up to 100 billion suns has vanished from the core of one of the universe's largest galaxies, likely catapulted entirely into deep space by gravitational waves.

claims.claim: Galaxy A2261-BCG spans approximately one million light-years across.
A2261-BCG is roughly ten times the diameter of the Milky Way galaxy.
A2261-BCG possesses a puffy core measuring about 10,000 light-years across, the largest galactic core ever observed.
A2261-BCG is the brightest and most massive galaxy in the Abell 2261 cluster.
Based on the galaxy's mass, astronomers expected a central supermassive black hole weighing between 3 billion and 100 billion times the mass of the Sun.
By comparison, the supermassive black hole at the center of the Milky Way has a mass of about 4 million suns.
Hubble observations showed no concentrated cusp of starlight at the center, revealing instead a diffuse fog of stars with fairly even intensity across the core.
The densest concentration of stars in A2261-BCG is located roughly 2,000 light-years away from the center of the galaxy.
Astronomers searched for X-ray signatures of material superheating and falling into a central black hole using Chandra observations from 1999 and 2004, but found nothing.
A deeper Chandra search using 2018 observations led by Kayhan Gultekin of the University of Michigan failed to find any significant X-ray signature of a growing black hole.
Astronomers analyzed radio observations using the Karl G. Jansky Very Large Array to search for black hole activity in the galaxy.
One leading explanation is that asymmetric gravitational waves from merging black holes kicked the resulting supermassive black hole completely out of the galactic core.
A recoiling supermassive black hole has never been definitively detected and remains hypothetical.
Abell 2261 was studied as part of the Cluster Lensing And Supernova survey with Hubble (CLASH).
Astronomers anticipated that the James Webb Space Telescope could help search for the missing black hole or confirm if it recoiled out of the center.

disputed: Distance to Abell 2261: S2 and S3 state 3 billion light-years, while S4, S5, S6, and S7 state approximately 2.7 billion light-years. Scripts should state 'between 2.7 and 3 billion light-years away'.
Age of prior radio activity: S5 states radio emission showed activity 50 million years ago, while S6 states roughly 48 million years ago. Scripts should attribute as 'around 50 million years ago'.
